As AI Takes on More Work, a Leader’s Responsibility Only Grows. Here’s Why.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Over the past few years, entrepreneurs have been living in a state of constant mobilization.
  • After several years of running this marathon, it might seem that we should finally be able to catch our breath.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past few years, entrepreneurs have been living in a state of constant mobilization. First came the pandemic, followed by geopolitical instability, shifting markets, the emergence of artificial intelligence and a new generation of technology-driven competitors.

After several years of running this marathon, it might seem that we should finally be able to catch our breath. Yet it is precisely now that we are beginning to realize that the pace of change is only accelerating.

We have become accustomed to looking for ways to manage stress: exercise, saunas, digital detoxes and meditation. But perhaps the problem is not simply how much time we spend resting. Perhaps the pace of change itself has fundamentally shifted.

According to recent reports, the defining feature of our time is the exponential development of technology. Today, we are no longer talking simply about digitalization, but about the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence. AI is ceasing to be a standalone tool and is beginning to shape the environment in which businesses operate. It accelerates analysis, automates processes, changes consumer expectations and reduces the cost of many operations.

But as opportunities grow, so does human responsibility.

In the past, a tech giant could operate for years based on a strategy chosen once and then followed consistently. Today, almost every change becomes a separate project: introducing artificial intelligence, modifying a product, restructuring sales channels or adapting to newly introduced customer habits. Entrepreneurs are no longer simply making decisions; they are constantly managing change.

In a recent development, uncertainty is increasingly becoming the environment in which businesses are built. The question for every entrepreneur is whether they can make decisions and take action under such conditions.

Sources indicate that I often say that entrepreneurship is not so much a profession as a state of mind. Education, planning and capital all help, but entrepreneurs must act with incomplete information, adapt, overcome setbacks and maintain the emotional balance required to lead others.

This is precisely why emotional intelligence matters so much. Strong analysts can be hired, but a leader must personally learn to manage their own reactions, understand others and communicate convincingly in stressful situations.

Sources indicate that A team takes its cues from its leader. If the leader freezes, the organization slows down. If they act recklessly, it risks losing discipline. The challenge is to remain calm without becoming passive, and optimistic without ignoring risks.

Sources indicate that persistence is equally notable: that inner drive that keeps you working until you achieve the desired result. At the same time, the tools and the route may change. It is important not to confuse persistence with stubbornness, or activity with actual progress.

Sources indicate that the paradox is that as AI takes over more routine tasks, the responsibility of leaders continues to grow. It is the human being who determines the direction of development, builds the team and assesses strategic risks. The ability to understand what is happening and adapt more promptly is therefore becoming a key competitive advantage.

Sources indicate that A leader can only step away from the controls when there are people around them capable of taking over. This makes one of the most key resources available to any leader the ability to build a strong team, establish trust with partners and delegate authority.

But there is a question that I believe is far more crucial than efficiency.

Sources indicate that we talk far too often about how to outperform competitors, increase market capitalization or scale a business. Almost never do we ask ourselves a different question: What is the ultimate purpose of being human?

You can defeat your competitors, build the largest company and achieve extraordinary results. Yet none of these things guarantees what matters most: a happy life.

Recent findings suggest that most people define their goals in terms of achievements. Almost nobody says: My primary goal is to build the happiest possible life for myself. Yet this is precisely the goal that determines the value of all other achievements!

Inner exhaustion is not always simply a matter of how much work we do. If the lifestyle we have chosen consistently leads to it, we should ask ourselves what goals we are pursuing. Perhaps something needs to change.

So perhaps the most useful advice for entrepreneurs today is surprisingly simple: Start by understanding yourself. Understand your genuine emotional needs, strengths, natural abilities and limitations. Do not try to become someone you are not. Do not build a career that goes against your own nature.

Recent findings suggest that people generally enjoy doing things they are good at. And they tend to become good at things they genuinely enjoy doing. When these two things coincide, the likelihood of success increases significantly.

This applies beyond business. Even philanthropy, traditionally regarded as an exclusively altruistic activity, naturally benefits the person who gives as well. The opportunity to share knowledge, help others and see the results of one’s actions all generate positive emotions. There is nothing wrong with that. It is simply human nature.

In general, many things become easier to understand when viewed through the lens of biology rather than conventional abstractions. Our emotions, motivation and sense of fulfillment have a very real physiological basis. Relationships with other people, meaningful work, the environment in which we live, our health and our ability to take pleasure in our own achievements — these are the elements that combine to create a sense of well-being.

According to recent reports, happiness, therefore, is neither a matter of luck nor a state of constant euphoria. It is a dynamic balance between the emotions a person genuinely needs and the states they experience at any given moment. This balance cannot be found once and preserved forever. It must be maintained continuously, with adjustments to our lives as the world around us changes.

And perhaps this is one of the greatest challenges of the age of artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that machines may become increasingly capable of analyzing data, writing code, creating content, automating processes and helping us make decisions. But help with a decision is not the same as responsibility for it. The question of why we are in business and what kind of life we want to live remains ours to answer.

That is why a leader’s true competitive advantage lies not only in the ability to use AI, but also in the ability to remain the author of their own life.

Technology may change the rules of the game many times over. The pace of change may accelerate, and artificial intelligence may take over a significant share of intellectual work. But responsibility for our own decisions, our own happiness and our own path will remain with us.

And perhaps this is the most valuable skill a leader can possess today: the ability to maintain inner strength and remain the author of their own life, even as the world around them changes faster than ever before.

Over the past few years, entrepreneurs have been living in a state of constant mobilization. First came the pandemic, followed by geopolitical instability, shifting markets, the emergence of artificial intelligence and a newly introduced generation of technology-driven competitors.

After several years of running this marathon, it might seem that we should finally be able to catch our breath. Yet it is precisely now that we are beginning to realize that the pace of change is only accelerating.

According to recent reports, we have become accustomed to looking for ways to manage stress: exercise, saunas, digital detoxes and meditation. But perhaps the problem is not simply how much time we spend resting. Perhaps the pace of change itself has fundamentally shifted.

Latest Update: Microsoft ‘To Do’ consumers make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm.
  • Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal owners that Microsoft To Do would be their new home.
  • It has been revealed that microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm.

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal owners that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

It has been revealed that microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the firm’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

In a recent development, the reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

Industry observers note that that’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The manufacturer stated putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Owners weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft declared Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

It has been revealed that rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

It has been revealed that the most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent firm, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist customers may end up back with the people who built it.

  • It has been revealed that the offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares of Anthropic closed up 17% in first-day trading Thursday amid an otherwise down day for the broader market.

Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing.

It has been revealed that the offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

It has been revealed that for the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier plan to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the firm.

It has been revealed that anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

According to recent reports, put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX, by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering.

The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books.

For the first nine months of the year, the firm had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago.

Industry observers note that anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

XRP’s price correction has continued, drawing the asset back to levels last seen during the November 2024 bear market while the broader crypto market continues to see intense selling pressure.

While market sentiment has shifted massively, the latest data on the Kalshi prediction market reveals that the odds of XRP experiencing deeper price losses this year have increased.

While XRP’s price correction has intensified with the asset posting a daily price decrease of over 8% in the last 24 hours, traders on Kalshi believe the volatility may be far from over.

As such, data shows that traders on the platform are increasingly betting on XRP retesting $0.7 before the year runs out, causing the probability of XRP falling back to that level to sit at 55% as of November 21.

With just over a month left before the year wraps up, XRP’s chances of defeating this bearish prediction are slim, as the asset has continued to struggle amid the market downturn, with retail and institutional demand presently on hold.

As XRP continues to show zero signs of recovery, data from CryptoRank demonstrates that the asset has posted a massive quarterly loss for Q4.

Even though the quarter has yet to run out, XRP has already suffered a price loss of 39% since October, the weakest quarterly return seen so far in 2026.

If momentum persists, XRP might be at risk of falling below the $0.7 mark as investor confidence is rapidly fading.

An SEO Expert’s 3 Tactics for Getting Your Business Found Beyond Google

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Sources indicate that for years, getting found online meant getting found on Google.
  • It has been revealed that those things still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that for years, getting found online meant getting found on Google. Businesses researched keywords, optimized their websites and built backlinks to attract potential customers.

It has been revealed that those things still matter. But today, someone might discover a business through ChatGPT, a LinkedIn post or a recommendation from someone they trust, without ever typing a query into Google.

Sources indicate that as an AI and SEO specialist running Create & Grow, a digital marketing agency, I’ve learned that many of the principles behind effective SEO work just as well beyond search engines. You need to understand what people are looking for, give them a reason to pay attention and build enough authority for them to trust you.

Here’s how I’ve applied those principles to client campaigns and my own business.

Keyword research tells you what people search for, but it doesn’t always reveal how they describe their problems.

Sources indicate that according to Salesforce’s State of the Connected Customer report, 73% of customers expect companies to understand their unique needs and expectations. To do that, businesses need to listen to customers, not just study search volumes.

I saw this firsthand while working with a client in the invoicing software industry.

According to recent reports, instead of relying exclusively on keyword tools, we analyzed the client’s support tickets, sales calls, live chats, customer reviews and internal search data. We wanted to understand how business owners described the problems that made them look for invoicing software in the first place.

They weren’t necessarily using technical phrases like “accounts receivable automation.” They talked about chasing late payments, making mistakes on invoices, wasting hours on repetitive tasks and struggling to predict cash flow.

That distinction shaped our strategy. Rather than promoting the software through generic accounting terminology, we focused on connecting the client’s brand to the specific problems its customers wanted to solve.

We built those associations through digital PR, guest articles, LinkedIn posts, company page optimization and relevant niche edits on third-party websites. We also prioritized branded links and mentions instead of focusing exclusively on keyword-rich backlinks.

According to recent reports, our outreach campaign generated a mix of dofollow and nofollow backlinks, as well as unlinked brand mentions. Our goal wasn’t simply to earn backlinks. We wanted the client’s brand to appear consistently in conversations about the problems its software addressed.

This matters beyond traditional search. Someone might ask ChatGPT, “What software can help me stop chasing unpaid invoices?” When credible websites repeatedly connect a brand with that problem, AI systems have more relevant context about what the tech giant offers.

That doesn’t guarantee a recommendation, but it makes the brand’s positioning clearer to both AI tools and potential customers.

Sources indicate that we applied the same thinking to the client’s website. We created customer case studies showing how the invoicing software solved real problems and made pricing publicly available so potential buyers could evaluate the product more easily. Both changes also made commercially useful information accessible to AI search tools.

After six months, the client’s organic traffic increased by almost 25%, ranking keywords grew by 31%, and keywords in Google’s Top 10 increased by 39%. Most importantly, organic demo requests rose by 44%.

Sources indicate that those results came from our combined SEO and brand-building efforts, not one isolated tactic. We also deliberately prioritized commercial intent over traffic volume. As AI-generated answers increasingly satisfy informational searches, attracting people actively evaluating invoicing solutions matters more than ranking for every broad accounting question.

It has been revealed that the same principle applies when you’re trying to get someone else’s attention. Before asking for anything, understand what that person might actually find valuable.

I put this into practice recently when I wanted to publish guest articles on a few high-authority websites.

Most guest-post outreach starts with a predictable request: “Do you accept guest contributions?” I wanted my message to stand out by showing editors exactly what they could gain from working with me.

So I researched relevant websites and contacted their editors and marketing managers with examples of articles I’d already published. These weren’t generic pieces that anyone could produce with an AI writing tool. They combined firsthand experience from real SEO campaigns, original insights, practical examples, research and relevant statistics.

I also made sure the articles were properly optimized for search, but the real selling point was the value they delivered to readers.

Then I indicated the results. I included evidence of the organic traffic those articles attracted, the keywords they ranked for on Google and the citations and brand mentions they earned in AI-generated answers.

Sources indicate that in other words, I wasn’t asking editors to imagine what I could deliver. I was showing them a finished example of the quality, expertise and measurable value I could bring to their websites.

Only then did I make my offer: “Would you like me to create something like this for your website, for free?”.

It has been revealed that that’s a very different proposition from asking someone for a backlink or a guest-post opportunity. The editor gets a thoroughly researched, experience-driven article that can attract relevant visitors and strengthen the website’s authority. I get an opportunity to demonstrate my expertise to a new audience.

Industry observers note that to reach people outside my existing network, I used LinkedIn Premium All-in-One, which includes InMail messaging. I didn’t need all 30 monthly InMail credits. Roughly 10 carefully targeted messages generated three client inquiries and one paying customer.

Some recipients became interested in my SEO consulting, content strategy and outreach services after seeing the work I could do. One manufacturer ultimately hired me to improve its outreach process and develop stronger pitches.

What’s interesting is that I hadn’t approached these people to sell SEO services. I led with proof of what I could create for them, made an offer that was genuinely useful and let the business conversation develop naturally.

In a recent development, that’s why I prefer carefully researched outreach over sending hundreds of generic messages. The objective isn’t to contact as many people as possible. It’s to make your offer so relevant and valuable that the recipient has a compelling reason to respond.

Sources indicate that one well-researched message can open a door. But consistently useful content can make people familiar with your work long before you ever contact them.

Sources indicate that that’s why I treat LinkedIn content planning much like SEO research. Before publishing, I study competing digital marketing agencies: their websites, LinkedIn posts and how they position their expertise. I look at which topics generate engagement, what questions their audiences ask and where their content leaves room for a better answer.

I use those insights to initiative content for my personal LinkedIn profile. Some posts share practical lessons about SEO, AI search and digital marketing, often drawn from my own campaigns. Others are deliberately more relaxed and humorous.

Industry observers note that the professional posts show people how I solve problems. The humorous ones make my content more relatable and give people another reason to engage. I don’t expect every post to generate a lead, and I certainly don’t want every post to read like a sales pitch.

According to recent reports, instead, I want people to recognize my work over time. And that has become a reliable source of conversations and client opportunities.

Sources indicate that some people reach out through LinkedIn messages after reading my posts. Others start conversations in the comments. I’ve also met people at conferences who tell me they’ve followed my content for years. We might talk about SEO, exchange ideas and stay in touch. Sometimes, months later, they contact me about a project and become clients.

By then, I don’t need to start by explaining who I am or convincing them that I understand SEO. They’ve already seen how I think, what I know and the results I share.

That matters because B2B buyers often develop preferences before contacting a provider. According to 6sense‘s 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report, in 77% of B2B purchases studied, buyers ended up choosing the organization they already preferred before their first sales conversation.

My experience illustrates why that matters in practice: Someone who has followed your work for a long time may already trust your expertise when they finally need your services.

The next step is making sure that first interaction doesn’t become the last. On LinkedIn, that might mean giving readers a reason to follow your personal profile or company page. Outside LinkedIn, an email newsletter can help you stay connected with website visitors. You could even build a private Slack community where people in your industry exchange ideas, ask questions and learn from one another.

It has been revealed that whatever channel you choose, the principle is the same: Offer enough value that people want to stay connected. Then keep showing up with content worth their attention.

SEO taught me to understand what customers need, pay attention to the competition and build authority through useful content. Those principles now help me get discovered through AI tools, LinkedIn and relationships that start well before a sales conversation.

In a recent development, you don’t need to abandon Google or be active on every platform. Start by speaking your customers’ language, approaching newly introduced contacts with something valuable and creating content that gives people a reason to keep following your work.

If you’re ready to make your business easier to find and harder to forget, LinkedIn’s Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to see which ones fit your strategy.

Recent findings suggest that getting discovered creates the opportunity. Being remembered and trusted is what turns that opportunity into business.

For years, getting found online meant getting found on Google. Businesses researched keywords, optimized their websites and built backlinks to attract potential customers.

Those things still matter. But today, someone might discover a business through ChatGPT, a LinkedIn post or a recommendation from someone they trust, without ever typing a query into Google.

As an AI and SEO specialist running Create & Grow, a digital marketing agency, I’ve learned that many of the principles behind effective SEO work just as well beyond search engines. You need to understand what people are looking for, give them a reason to pay attention and build enough authority for them to trust you.

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

According to recent reports, testing that more closely replicates the tech giant’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company notes it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

Recent findings suggest that what set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

Recent findings suggest that the bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows revision used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

Industry observers note that so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

In a recent development, the final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

Recent findings suggest that first, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Industry observers note that second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

In a recent development, third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report indicates.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate matter.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

It has been revealed that once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft notes it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft notes it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also intends to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

It has been revealed that some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Sources indicate that microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it prepares to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft mentioned the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it claims. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

Industry observers note that the fresh testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the firm says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the store is finally quiet. Even though the last customer has left, the owner’s laptop is still open, and their to-do list is overwhelmingly long. There’s still one more email to answer, one more thing to do.

According to recent reports, buying a gift for that person, the small business owner or entrepreneur with a lot on their plate, can be surprisingly difficult. Another motivational mug might elicit a smile, but it will probably not make Monday easier. A more thoughtful choice is something that fits the way they actually work.

According to recent reports, that is the thinking behind these 10 gift ideas. Rather than treating every entrepreneur as a startup founder glued to a laptop, this list considers several kinds of working days. There are options for people building a business from the kitchen table.

Black Friday adds another consideration. Is a useful gift genuinely available for less? Amazon’s current sale coverage includes discounts on headphones, microphones, computer accessories and other work-friendly technology.

The right choice still depends on the recipient. The most meaningful gift shows that you have noticed the person behind the business.

Here are the 10 best gifts for entrepreneurs.

Square Terminal: For the business owner ready to simplify checkout.

Sources indicate that square Terminal combines sales, card payments and receipt-printing in one device. It’s a practical gift candidate for a store owner who wants to bundle those tasks together. Its built-in battery also allows cordless use around the business rather than keeping every transaction tied to one spot. Before ordering, ask if the recipient wants to use Square and if this terminal fits their existing setup. This product is at the moment over 10% off, making the final price $265.

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite, 16GB: For the entrepreneur who has time to read.

This Kindle Paperwhite has a seven-inch glare-free display, 16GB of storage and battery life of up to 12 weeks. For an entrepreneur, this gift could allow them to read a biography on a flight, return to a novel after closing the shop or finally start the book a friend recommended. Its appeal is especially clear for someone who already reads digitally but would appreciate a separate reading device. Think twice before buying if the person is devoted to paper books or has never expressed an interest in e-readers. This Kindle is $70 off for Black Friday, making it $130 total.

reMarkable Paper Pro bundle with Marker Plus and black leather Book Folio: For the handwritten thinker.

Sources indicate that some entrepreneurs think best by writing things out. They sketch a initiative or rewrite a sentence until the argument becomes clear. The reMarkable Paper Pro is aimed at that style of work, with an 11.8-inch color display and adjustable reading light. It is a color e-ink paper tablet that doubles as a digital notebook for writing and drawing. The requested package includes the Marker Plus pen and black leather Book Folio. As a gift, it makes the most sense for someone whose working day already involves handwritten notes, like a founder mapping a latest service. This package is $100 off for Black Friday, making the final price about $700.

Bose QuietComfort Bluetooth Headphones: For the entrepreneur looking for some peace and quiet.

It has been revealed that bose QuietComfort headphones offer active noise cancellation, a built-in microphone and up to 24 hours of playback. That makes them a thoughtful choice for someone who regularly works around other people. The headphones also allow the recipient to use them for music or listening to podcasts or e-books during time off. Make sure to consider whether the recipient mentioned wanting over-ear headphones and if they already wear a pair throughout the day. Only some colors have the Black Friday discount, which is 53%, or $190 off, for a final price of $169.

Gloryang 668BT thermal shipping-label printer: For the seller packing orders at home.

In a recent development, the Gloryang 668BT prints standard 4-by-6-inch shipping labels and supports label widths from one to 4.4 inches. Its Bluetooth and USB connections support use with phones, tablets and computers. This is a useful device for a small shop owner who has mentioned that their labeling process needs improvement. It’s also compact and is 25% off for Black Friday, for a final price of $43.

Anker Laptop Power Bank: For the entrepreneur who always needs a charger.

It has been revealed that their laptop battery runs out of charge just as a client meeting begins, and their phone is nearly dead too. A business owner who works across shared spaces and cafes could find a portable charger to be a thoughtful gift. This charger is a strong gift for a consultant or founder who regularly carries several devices. A Black Friday deal brings the price of this charger below $100, at 32% off, which is a 90-day low price. It costs about $91.

Shure SM7B dynamic vocal microphone: For the owner building a podcast.

According to recent reports, this gift is for a business owner who records interviews, lessons or a podcast. The Shure SM7B is a dynamic vocal microphone designed for uses including podcasting, broadcast and recording. Its pickup pattern focuses on sound in front of the microphone. The SM7B uses an XLR connection rather than a direct USB connection; the XLR is better for sound quality. The microphone is $70 off for Black Friday, bringing its price to $369 at the time of writing.

Apple Magic Mouse with USB-C: For the Apple user who wants a clean-looking accessory.

Apple’s Magic Mouse is wireless and rechargeable. Its Multi-Touch surface supports gestures such as scrolling through documents and swiping between web pages. The USB-C version includes a charging cable, and Apple says its battery can last about a month or more between charges. This is a good gift for an entrepreneur who already likes Apple’s mouse design. The clean accessory is a safe option if the recipient currently uses a Magic Mouse and wants another for a second workspace. The white color is on sale for $20 off this Black Friday, making its price about $60.

Soundcore P30i noise-cancelling earbuds: For an affordable, useful everyday gift.

Sources indicate that the Soundcore P30i earbuds offer noise cancellation and a charging case that doubles as a phone stand. The product listing also advertises up to 45 hours of total playback. The phone-stand feature adds a small practical touch. Their size makes them a reasonable candidate for someone who prefers carrying earbuds rather than over-ear headphones. They are perfect for listening during a commute. The earbuds were originally listed for about $50 but are more than 50% off for Black Friday, bringing the price down to $24.

Soundcore Select 4 Go Bluetooth speaker: For making the workday a little more enjoyable.

A small speaker can be a welcome addition to the hours spent working in a store or office. The Soundcore Select 4 Go is a compact Bluetooth speaker with a five-watt output. Its product listing advertises up to 20 hours of playback and an IP67 water- and dust-resistance rating. It is the ideal gift for an entrepreneur who likes having music nearby as they move between different working spaces. A Black Friday deal slashes the price to a 365-day low, making it $20 when it was originally $35.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 10:09 amNovember 21, 2026 at 10:13 am.

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley, a GeekWire contributing writer, sizes up where the organization stands after one of its most eventful weeks in years.

According to recent reports, microsoft opened its Ignite conference with an apology for the global Outlook outage, then took direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic on price, even though it invests in both and sells their models. We discuss the lasting damage from the outage, why enterprise customers have few places to go even when they’re fed up, and Microsoft’s pitch to make Copilot the “OS for work,” as Anthropic goes public.

Mary Jo also explains how Microsoft changed the way it rolls out news at its big conferences, what got lost along the way, and what that states about the company after the shakeup of its communications team. Plus, we weigh who from Microsoft could lead Nvidia, and the GeekWire trivia challenge goes back to 1997.

It has been revealed that edited by Curt Milton. Music by Daniel L.K. Caldwell.

#167658. Tech Report: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Reveals Us Why

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (987 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crunchbase ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Reveals Us Why

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant.
  • Sources indicate that we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model.
  • Recent findings suggest that the SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value.

Sources indicate that we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a tech giant that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it.

Recent findings suggest that the SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value.

It has been revealed that this pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal.

The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked.

It has been revealed that when OpenAI debuted ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025.

In a recent development, the market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were unveiled later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal.

According to recent reports, from there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year.

Industry observers note that as an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others.

It has been revealed that there were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole.

That is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April.

At my firm, Oxx, we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back.

In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike, whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October.

Industry observers note that the knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash.

Industry observers note that it produced the unintended consequence of driving firm ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value.

The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private firm transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem.

Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx, a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale.

It has been revealed that impersonation scams are quietly growing across the crypto space, with one of the most troubling tactics seen being the deepfake: lifelike, AI-generated impersonations of crypto executives and employees soliciting money on video calls that look and sound real enough to make anyone hesitate. The personas are fabricated, but the sophistication is genuine.

Every day, people are contacted by impersonators using the names, likenesses, and even job titles of crypto personnel, including Binance staff, to solicit investments or financial transactions via WhatsApp, Telegram, and other channels.

Binance stated that scammers prey on people's growing interest in investing and digital finance and on their trust, often masquerading as its employees or executives to exploit its credibility.

With advances in AI and deepfake technology, they can create personas that look and sound real. Crypto customers are therefore urged to beware of unsolicited advice or "special opportunities" and to refrain from clicking on unknown links or URLs.

Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

It has been revealed that according to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Industry observers note that those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

It has been revealed that denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

In a recent development, timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Recent findings suggest that node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

According to recent reports, finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

According to recent reports, contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec states it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

It has been revealed that denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • Sources indicate that attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Sources indicate that attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals matter ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

It has been revealed that each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a fresh router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal revision at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Sources indicate that last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

Recent findings suggest that AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella states his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the Newly introduced York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

Sources indicate that the FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

According to recent reports, it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t revision for the next five to 10 years.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

Industry observers note that there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines.
  • So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows.
  • Industry observers note that to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

Industry observers note that to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Recent findings suggest that much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old tech giant raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor claims it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a Fresh York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In a recent development, in this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old tech giant picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

According to recent reports, agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Recent findings suggest that not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t strategy for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, states Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it notes it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the firm,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s notable that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

In a recent development, these may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Firm earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”).

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

Cardano fell to $0.133, a five-month low on Saturday as the crypto market sell-off deepened. At the time of writing, Cardano had slightly rebounded, up 1.82% in the last 24 hours to $0.144, as a substantial buy wall of 3.96 million ADA emerged on Binance, offering a layer of support as sellers pressured the cryptocurrency.

A buy wall occurs when a large volume of buy orders is concentrated around a particular price level on an exchange's order book. Such an order cluster can indicate that traders are prepared to purchase an asset at that price, potentially slowing further declines if selling pressure meets sufficient demand.

In Cardano's case, the 3.96 million ADA order cluster that occurred below the $0.14 level revealed a notable level of buying interest. As the orders at this level were filled, they helped absorb selling pressure for Cardano and provided short-term support for the price.

Current data from CoinGlass indicates that open interest is down 1.98%, mostly due to shorts closing, although funding remains negative at −0.0099%, with shorts paying longs.

The next key levels to watch for ADA, according to on-chain data provided by CoinGlass, are $0.1462, which has a short liquidation cluster, and $0.1375, which has a long liquidation cluster.

Dijkstra hard fork preparations continue to progress, with Intersect, a Cardano-based entity, revealing what might come next in the coming weeks.

in about one or two weeks, the Cardano Node 11.2.3 release (GitHub), the Node RC 2026w47 release for the Musashi network (GitHub), and the publication of v6 of CAP-12 to the Constitutional Amendment Portal are anticipated.

In about two to three weeks, the Cardano Node 11.3 pre-release is anticipated, while an revision to the Constitution governance action on-chain is expected in about one month.

Sources indicate that dijkstra requires both constitutional and technical changes in the era of on-chain governance. These include Constitutional guardrails (Enhancement Constitution) and Plutus V4 (Parameter Update).

CAP-12 "Dijkstra era parameters" proposes to amend the Constitution to accommodate latest block type definitions and set guardrails for new updatable parameter types introduced with Protocol Version 12.
